nameStory: Thomson's Rosette Lichen gets its first name from James Thomson, a 19th-century Scottish botanist who studied lichens extensively. The "rosette" part describes its beautiful circular growth pattern, where the flat lobes radiate outward from the center like the petals of a rose or the leaves of a garden rosette.
description: Thomson's Rosette Lichen is a crusty, flat lichen that forms neat circular patches on tree bark and rocks. It grows in distinctive rosette patterns, with gray-green lobes spreading outward from a central point like spokes on a wheel. Each rosette typically reaches about 1-3 inches across, though multiple rosettes often grow together to form larger colonies. Like all lichens, it's actually two organisms living together - a fungus and an algae working as a team.

idTips.label: Rosette Growth Pattern
idTips.description: Forms perfect circular patches with lobes radiating from the center like flower petals - run your finger gently around the edge to feel the individual flat segments

idTips.label: Lobe Tips
idTips.description: The outer edges of lobes are often slightly darker and may have tiny black dots (fruiting bodies) - these feel smooth and slightly raised when touched

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Upper surface feels smooth to slightly rough, with a matte finish rather than shiny - no powdery coating that rubs off on your fingers

idTips.label: Color Pattern
idTips.description: Pale gray-green to whitish center gradually darkening toward the lobe tips, creating a subtle gradient effect across the rosette

idTips.label: Attachment
idTips.description: Sits fairly flat against its surface with edges that may curl up slightly - difficult to peel off without damaging the lichen

habitat: Thomson's Rosette Lichen grows on the bark of deciduous trees, particularly favoring smooth-barked species like maples, birches, and ash trees in New England's forests. You'll most often spot it in mature woodlands and along forest edges where there's good air circulation. It tends to prefer slightly more protected spots than some of its relatives, often growing a few feet up tree trunks rather than right at ground level.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more noticeable as snow melts and humidity increases, often appearing brighter and more vibrant after winter dormancy. Look for small black fruiting structures beginning to develop.
seasonality.summer: Growth is active during humid periods, though hot dry spells may cause it to appear duller and more contracted. The rosette pattern is most clearly defined during this season.
seasonality.fall: Often produces its most prominent reproductive structures (small black dots) as cooler, moister conditions return. Colors may become more muted but patterns remain clear.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible year-round but appears darker and more contracted against tree bark. Snow cover may obscure ground-level specimens, making trunk colonies easier to spot.

funFact: Thomson's Rosette Lichen can actually "hold its breath" during dry spells - it shuts down all biological activity and can survive months without water, then spring back to life within minutes of getting wet, like a biological sponge that's been waiting for rain!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other rosette lichens in the Physcia genus, especially Star Rosette Lichen which has more pointed, star-like lobes, and Hoary Rosette Lichen which has a distinctly powdery white coating. Memory trick: Thomson's has the most "perfect" circular rosettes - think "Thomson's tidy circles."
contextualKnowledge: With only 8 recorded observations in New England, Thomson's Rosette Lichen is quite uncommon in our region, making any sighting noteworthy for citizen science projects. The Physcia genus can be tricky for beginners since many species look similar, so don't worry if identification feels challenging - even experienced naturalists sometimes need a magnifying glass and field guides to tell them apart confidently.
compareHints: Thomson's Rosette Lichen differs from its Physcia relatives by having the most regularly circular, "tidy" rosettes without the pronounced star-like points of P. stellaris or the powdery coating of P. aipolia. Its lobes tend to be broader and more evenly spaced than the narrow, crowded lobes of P. tenella, and it lacks the distinctly hooded lobe tips found in P. adscendens.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its rosette lichen relatives, this species stands out for having the coarsest, most abundant soredia concentrated along the lobe margins.
Among the rosette lichens, Star Rosette Lichen stands out for its exceptionally clean, star-like growth pattern and complete lack of surface textures.
Among its rosette lichen relatives, Hooded Rosette Lichen stands out for its distinctly upward-curling lobe tips, while Star Rosette Lichen has flatter, more star-like projections.

Among its rosette lichen relatives, the Hoary Rosette Lichen is distinguished by its particularly pale, almost silvery-blue coloration compared to the darker grays of species like Star Rosette Lichen.

Blue-gray rosette lichen stands out from its Physcia relatives primarily by its blue-gray soredia - those powdery reproductive bumps that other rosette lichens either lack or have in different colors.
Black-eyed rosette lichen differs from its Physcia relatives primarily by having more prominent and consistently dark apothecia compared to species like star rosette lichen or hoary rosette lichen.

Among its rosette lichen relatives, Fringed Rosette Lichen is distinguished by its combination of narrow lobes and fringed edges - Star Rosette Lichen has broader lobes without fringe, while Hooded Rosette Lichen has distinctive hood-shaped reproductive structures on the lobe tips.
Unlike Star Rosette Lichen which has more pointed, star-like lobes, Powder-tipped Rosette Lichen has broader lobes with those telltale white powdery tips.
Slender rosette lichen stands out from its Physcia relatives primarily by its notably narrow lobes - most other rosette lichens have broader, more substantial-looking lobes.
American Rosette Lichen differs from Star Rosette Lichen by having more powder on its surface and less distinct dark centers.
